column267: My first instance of racial discrimination that I can remember occurred at a public pool in Indianapolis, Indiana. The year would have been 1976 or there about. I was 10 or 11 at the time and supposedly spending the summer with my older sister. She was only two years out college and had no time to waste on a little trouble maker like me. So she dumped me off on her future husbands mother and I instead spent the summer with another little trouble maker my same age, who shared my love of dirt, swimming, and dogs. So fast forward to my first day at the local public pool. We show up and the first thing I notice is that the little kid end at this pool is enormous and bursting at the seams with my people, little trouble makers. Iâ€™m all in, my buddy though is a little nervous. What I donâ€™t notice, and what had never occurred to me before, is that we are the only two minorities at the pool. She is bi-racial Filipino and African American, Iâ€™m rocking a head full of bead tipped cornrows. Sheâ€™s nervous because maybe she had been exposed to racism before or maybe sheâ€™s just shy of crowds, whatever the reason she became reticent but I drag her to the showers so we can get into water. Everything is fine until someone bumps me and pulls one of my braids. I turn around to wrestle because thatâ€™s what bumping and hair pulling signals, and he hits me with the N word. I know what it means but Iâ€™ve never been called that but if he wanted to get down like that okay I was ready to get down. My response was the same one you hear on every play ground in every urban setting in US. â€œYour mammy is the N wordâ€ That response is usually a guarantee that blows will be thrown, and they were. My brother told my to always let them throw the first blow. It took me a while until I realized that I didnâ€™t have to actually take that punch. Lucky for me that only months earlier my brother took it upon himself to make sure that I could defend myself, especially against boys bigger than me. Iâ€™m extremely short, but my mouth is extremely flippant. He knew that with him away at boot camp, I would need some martial skills of my own. I proceeded to show little big man what a real butt whipping looked like and invited his mammy to come and get some of what he just got. It was my last time at that particular pool. My friendship with Angie was cemented. It was to last for decades. When I look back at that encounter, I think that Angie was used to being afraid of angering the bullies at the pool. She was tall enough that she made two of me, but there was no backing down in me because I didnâ€™t understand enough to be afraid. Some background information: Angieâ€™s family was the only black family in that neighborhood. She was an only child being raised by her grandparents. She was the only black child at her elementary school. I was born in Los Angeles in a mixed race neighborhood into a huge family. We vacationed in Baja and the YucatÃ¡n. When we moved to outside of Chicago, the neighborhood was still mixed race. It later became mostly black due to white flight. So even though I lived in urban areas my entire life, I was the one sheltered from the ugliness that is racism. Later in life, I was often the only black person, or only female person in school or on jobs. While I was never afraid, I noticed the difference in how I was addressed or even if I was acknowledged at all. I cannot thank my brother enough for making every effort to raise my as a boy instead of the very dirty, dog smelling, tiny girl that I was.
